title: The Counting Tower Adventure
markdown:
One sun-drenched afternoon Etta the explorer stood at the edge of the Whispering Woods with Moss the hedgehog and Nana Bea. The woods were a rustling green wall. Etta’s feather-topped hat bobbed.

“A tower,” she declared. “The tallest ever built, to peek over those leaves and see what is hiding.”

They gathered a pile of smooth, colourful wooden blocks from Nana Bea’s garden shed. Some were bright red like plump berries, some sunny yellow like dandelions, others a deep forest green. Etta started stacking. Plop, plop, plop. Moss, nose twitching, added his own. Wiggle, wobble, stack. He loved making things a bit wobbly. Nana Bea placed hers carefully, making sure each sat just so.

Soon they each had a tower, standing proudly. Then came the puzzle.

“Mine looks taller,” squeaked Moss, his nose going so fast it looked like a blurry raindrop.

“No, mine is. See how it tickles the sky?” Etta pointed. Her tower did seem to reach quite far.

Nana Bea tilted her head. “They look a bit different. Etta’s is very straight and tall. Moss’s has a little lean.”

They poked and prodded, trying to eyeball it from different angles. Etta stretched her arm up beside her tower. Moss stood on tiptoe next to his, balancing as if the ground might change its mind. It was all a bit confusing.

“How do we know for sure?” Moss mumbled. A tiny furrow appeared between his hedgehog eyebrows. He let out a sigh that rustled his quills.

Nana Bea picked up one single bright red block. She did not gather anyone around. “Let’s try something different. Think like explorers, but with our numbers.” She pointed to Etta’s tower. “How many blocks did you use, Etta? How many exactly?”

Etta blinked. “I didn’t count them. I just stacked them as high as I could until I ran out.”

Nana Bea pointed to Moss’s wobblier tower. “And you, Moss?”

Moss shuffled his little feet. “Me neither. I kept adding until it felt tall and wobbly and finished.” He gave a little wiggle to show how wobbly it was.

Nana Bea smiled. “What if we count them? Then we’ll know for sure. No guessing.”

She picked up a block from Etta’s tower. “One.” She added a sunny yellow one. “Two.” She continued, carefully lifting each block. “Three, four, five, six, seven, eight…” She set the last green one down. “Nine blocks for Etta’s tower.”

Etta’s eyes lit up like fireflies. “Nine. That’s a lot of blocks.”

They turned to Moss’s tower. Nana Bea gently counted each of his. “One, two, three… only six for Moss’s tower.”

Moss looked a little sad again. Another tiny sigh. He looked at Etta’s tower, which had more blocks.

“That’s okay, Moss,” Etta said quickly. She scooped up a handful of the leftover colourful blocks. “That means we have even more blocks to use. Let’s build a new tower. A team tower. Then we can really see over the woods.”

They put all the blocks together. Etta stacked carefully, making sure each block was level. Moss nudged blocks into place with his nose. Nana Bea checked each layer was steady. As they built, they counted, voices blending.

“Ten… eleven… twelve…” Etta called.

“Thirteen… fourteen…” Moss chirped.

“Fifteen… sixteen… seventeen…” Nana Bea added.

They kept going. Eighteen. Nineteen. When they finished, they looked at their sturdy tower. It was not just tall. It was exactly twenty blocks, stacked cleanly, reaching up, up, up. They stood on tiptoe and peered over the top.

There they were. The very tops of the Whispering Woods, and beyond, a field of sparkling bluebells like a carpet of sapphire.

“We did it,” cheered Etta. “Our tower is twenty blocks high. And look. The bluebell field.”

Moss bounced, quills standing straight up. “Twenty. That’s more than nine or six.” He did a little somersault of glee and then sat down hard, because somersaults and quills are a tricky mix.

Nana Bea beamed. She did not give a speech about why counting is helpful. She set the leftover red block at the base like a doorstep. “Nine, then six, then twenty when we join the piles. The numbers told us what our eyes only guessed.”

Etta looked at the colourful tower, then at her friends. “When we wanted to know which was taller, counting was the answer. It tells the real size, not just how it looks.”

Moss nodded, nose twitching. He did not wonder how many leaves were on a tree. He counted the bluebells he could see from the top — one, two, three — until he lost them in the blue, and that was enough.

The sun dipped low, painting the sky orange and pink. They sat by the twenty-block tower while it held still, a useful height, not a sermon. Moss leaned his quills carefully against the bottom layer. Etta tucked her hat under her arm so the feather would not tickle the top and spoil the count.
